questions.q: At the organizational level, what are the four functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?
options: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
Plan, Build, Test, Deploy
Scope, Exploit, Report, Retest
Collect, Clean, Train, Serve
questions.explain: The AI RMF runs as a continuous loop — Govern (policy/accountability), Map (context and risks of a specific system), Measure (evidence from testing), and Manage (acting on findings over the lifecycle).

questions.q: Under the EU AI Act's risk-tiered structure, what happens to a system classified as 'high-risk' (e.g. used in employment or credit scoring)?
options: It is banned outright with no path to deployment
It faces no additional obligations beyond existing law
It only needs to disclose that users are talking to an AI system
It faces the heaviest obligations: documented risk management, conformity assessments, and human oversight requirements
questions.explain: High-risk systems under the EU AI Act must meet the heaviest compliance bar — documented risk management, conformity assessment, human oversight, and detailed technical documentation before deployment.

questions.q: What distinguishes 'minimal risk' systems from 'limited risk' systems under the EU AI Act?
options: Minimal-risk systems face no additional obligations, while limited-risk systems (like chatbots) face transparency obligations such as disclosing that users are interacting with AI
Minimal-risk systems are banned outright, while limited-risk systems require conformity assessments
There is no difference — both tiers face identical obligations under the Act
Minimal-risk systems require human oversight, while limited-risk systems do not
questions.explain: Limited-risk systems carry transparency obligations (disclosing AI interaction, labeling AI-generated content), while minimal-risk systems — the majority of AI use cases — face no additional obligations under the Act.

questions.q: How does ISO/IEC 42001 differ from the NIST AI RMF and the EU AI Act?
options: It is identical to the EU AI Act and simply uses a different name for the same legal obligations
It replaces the need for any risk assessment process within an organization
It is a published, independently certifiable international standard for an AI management system, unlike the voluntary NIST guidance or the binding EU law
It only applies to organizations with fewer than ten employees
questions.explain: ISO/IEC 42001 is the AI-specific counterpart to ISO/IEC 27001 for information security — a certifiable management-system standard, distinct from NIST's voluntary framework and the EU's binding regulation.

questions.q: What is the actual function of a cross-functional AI governance board, as described in this lesson?
options: To rubber-stamp every AI system without reviewing its risk tier or evidence
To review each AI system against its risk tier, its RMF-based risk evidence, and its management-system documentation, before and after deployment
To write code for every AI system the organization deploys
To replace the need for red-teaming or threat modeling entirely
questions.explain: A real governance board reviews a system's EU AI Act risk tier, whether Map/Measure work (including red-teaming and threat modeling) has actually been done, and whether documentation holds up against a certified management system — not a one-time formality.
